question_text: A particle is moving $30^\circ$ north of east with speed $6\text{ m/s}$. After $3\text{ s}$ the particle is found to be moving along north with same speed. The magnitude of average acceleration in this interval of time is
diagram_description: A compass direction diagram showing North (N) and East (E) axes. An initial velocity vector $\vec{v}$ is directed at an angle of $30^\circ$ North of East, and a final velocity vector $\vec{v}$ of equal magnitude is directed due North.
solution:
Let the East direction be along the $+x$-axis (unit vector $\hat{i}$) and the North direction be along the $+y$-axis (unit vector $\hat{j}$).

Initial velocity:
$$\vec{v}_i = 6\cos 30^\circ\hat{i} + 6\sin 30^\circ\hat{j} = 6\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)\hat{i} + 6\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)\hat{j} = 3\sqrt{3}\hat{i} + 3\hat{j}$$

Final velocity:
$$\vec{v}_f = 6\hat{j}$$

Change in velocity:
$$\Delta \vec{v} = \vec{v}_f - \vec{v}_i = 6\hat{j} - (3\sqrt{3}\hat{i} + 3\hat{j}) = -3\sqrt{3}\hat{i} + 3\hat{j}$$

The magnitude of the change in velocity is:
$$|\Delta \vec{v}| = \sqrt{(-3\sqrt{3})^2 + 3^2} = \sqrt{27 + 9} = \sqrt{36} = 6\text{ m/s}$$

Alternatively, using $|\Delta \vec{v}| = 2v\sin\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)$ where the angle between initial and final velocity is $\theta = 90^\circ - 30^\circ = 60^\circ$:
$$|\Delta \vec{v}| = 2(6)\sin(30^\circ) = 6\text{ m/s}$$

The magnitude of the average acceleration is:
$$a_{\text{avg}} = \frac{|\Delta \vec{v}|}{\Delta t} = \frac{6\text{ m/s}}{3\text{ s}} = 2\text{ m/s}^2$$

question_text: To a stationary man, rain is falling on his back with a velocity $v$ at an angle $\theta$ with vertical. To make the rain velocity perpendicular to the man, he
options: Must move forward with a velocity $v\sin\theta$
Must move forward with a velocity $v\tan\theta$
Must move forward with a velocity $v\cos\theta$
Should move in the backward direction
solution:
Let the forward direction of the man be along the $+x$-axis and the vertically upward direction be along the $+y$-axis.

Since rain falls on his back at an angle $\theta$ with the vertical, the velocity of the rain relative to the ground is:
$$\vec{v}_r = v\sin\theta\,\hat{i} - v\cos\theta\,\hat{j}$$

Let the man move forward with velocity $\vec{v}_m = v_m\,\hat{i}$.

The relative velocity of rain with respect to the man is:
$$\vec{v}_{r/m} = \vec{v}_r - \vec{v}_m = (v\sin\theta - v_m)\,\hat{i} - v\cos\theta\,\hat{j}$$

For the relative velocity of the rain to appear perpendicular to the man's direction of motion (i.e., purely vertical along $-\hat{j}$):
$$v\sin\theta - v_m = 0 \implies v_m = v\sin\theta$$

Therefore, he must move forward with a velocity of $v\sin\theta$.

question_text: Three forces each of magnitude $1\text{ N}$ act along the sides $AB$, $BC$ and $CD$ of a regular hexagon. Magnitude of their resultant is
diagram_description: A regular hexagon $ABCDEF$. Three vectors of equal magnitude $1\text{ N}$ are drawn along the sides $AB$, $BC$, and $CD$, directed from $A$ to $B$, $B$ to $C$, and $C$ to $D$ respectively.
solution:
By the polygon law of vector addition, the resultant of the three vectors representing the consecutive sides $\vec{AB}$, $\vec{BC}$, and $\vec{CD}$ is given by:
$$\vec{R} = \vec{AB} + \vec{BC} + \vec{CD} = \vec{AD}$$

In a regular hexagon with side length $a$, the main diagonal $AD$ connects opposite vertices and passes through the center. Its length is twice the side length:
$$AD = 2a$$

Given the magnitude of each force is $a = 1\text{ N}$:
$$|\vec{R}| = |\vec{AD}| = 2 \times 1\text{ N} = 2\text{ N}$$

question_text: If unit vector $\hat{j}$ is rotated through an angle of $45^\circ$ anticlockwise, then new vector obtained is
solution:
The unit vector $\hat{j}$ lies along the positive $y$-axis, which is at an angle of $90^\circ$ with the positive $x$-axis.

When it is rotated anticlockwise by $45^\circ$, its new angle with the positive $x$-axis becomes:
$$\theta = 90^\circ + 45^\circ = 135^\circ$$

Since rotating a unit vector preserves its magnitude ($|\vec{u}| = 1$), the components of the new vector are:
$$\vec{u} = \cos(135^\circ)\,\hat{i} + \sin(135^\circ)\,\hat{j}$$

Using $\cos(135^\circ) = -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$ and $\sin(135^\circ) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$:
$$\vec{u} = -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\,\hat{i} + \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\,\hat{j}$$
